items.title: The Crystal Palace (Hyde Park)
items.description: Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace was built in Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition as a glass-and-iron structure. Standardised prefabricated parts enabled rapid assembly; horizontal girders and cast-iron columns supported wooden glazing bars and extensive glazing. Completed shortly before the exhibition opened, it is distinct from the substantially rebuilt palace at Sydenham.
items.dateMeaning: Completion and opening of the original Hyde Park building (January and May 1851); design/construction began in 1850. Proposed timeline anchor preserves the existing 1851 date.

items.title: Sagrada Família
items.artist: Francisco de Paula del Villar; Antoni Gaudí (from 1883)
items.description: Construction of Barcelona’s Sagrada Família began in 1882 to diocesan architect Francisco de Paula del Villar’s neo-Gothic design. Antoni Gaudí took over in 1883 and transformed the project into a more ambitious design. The basilica remains under construction; its present form reflects work by successive generations, not Gaudí alone.
items.dateMeaning: Construction began in 1882; this is not a completion date. Gaudí took over the project in 1883. Construction remains ongoing.

items.title: Hôtel Solvay
items.description: Commissioned by industrialist Armand Solvay, this Brussels townhouse is Victor Horta's most lavish Art Nouveau masterpiece. It seamlessly integrates exposed ironwork, dynamic whiplash curves, and over two dozen varieties of marble into a unified work of art.

items.title: Paris Métro Entrances
items.description: Designed for the 1900 Paris World's Fair, these cast-iron modular station entrances brought Art Nouveau aesthetics into public transit. Their organic, plant-like forms and glowing amber glass lamps transformed everyday urban infrastructure into decorative art.

items.title: Bauhaus Building Dessau
items.description: The physical embodiment of modern architectural theory. Its asymmetrical pinwheel plan, steel skeleton frame, and famous continuous glass curtain wall eliminated load-bearing exterior walls, establishing a new functionalist aesthetic.

items.title: Barcelona Pavilion
items.artist: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich
items.description: Designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich as Germany’s pavilion for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition, the building combined glass, steel, and marble. Its spatial composition and carefully assembled materials became influential in modern architecture. The original was dismantled after the exposition; the pavilion now standing on the site is a reconstruction opened in 1986.
items.dateMeaning: Original pavilion designed for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition; the surviving building is a reconstruction opened in 1986. Design/start/completion dates for the original are not separately established by this source.

items.title: Chrysler Building
items.description: William Van Alen designed the 77-story Chrysler Building for Walter P. Chrysler in New York. Its ornament incorporated automobile imagery, including hubcaps, fenders and enlarged eagle radiator caps. A metal-clad spire capped the building, which rose to 1,046 feet and held the world-height title from 1930 to 1931.
items.dateMeaning: Existing 1930 anchor retained as the documented world-height-title milestone; construction began 19 September 1928. Exact opening/legal completion date remains unverified in the fetched packet.

items.title: Villa Savoye
items.description: A manifesto of Modernist architecture that visually codified Le Corbusier's 'Five Points of Architecture': pilotis support columns, a roof garden, an open floor plan, ribbon windows, and a free facade.

items.title: Empire State Building
items.description: Designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon Associates, the 102-story Empire State Building rose in New York between March 17, 1930, and May 1, 1931. The official history describes a pace of about 4.5 stories per week. Construction completion and public opening were distinct milestones: the building opened on May 1, 1931.
items.dateMeaning: Official opening on 1 May 1931; the institutional source places construction between 17 March 1930 and 1 May 1931. No unfetched exact physical-completion date is asserted.

items.title: Fallingwater
items.description: Designed as a weekend residence for the Kaufmann family, Fallingwater places its main house directly above Bear Run’s waterfall. Wright arranged cantilevered concrete terraces around a central stone chimney mass, echoing the nearby rock ledges. The design’s indoor-outdoor continuity and integration with its woodland setting are central to its organic-architecture approach.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; guest house construction followed in 1939 (main house construction 1936–38).

items.title: Edith Farnsworth House
items.description: Commissioned by Dr. Edith Farnsworth as a rural weekend home, the house was completed in 1951 after construction began in 1950. Mies van der Rohe set two horizontal slabs between which expansive glass walls open the interior to its wooded floodplain setting. The free-flowing living spaces surround a solid central core; the building is an expression of the International Style.
items.dateMeaning: Original completion date (not design date or construction start); construction began in 1950.

items.title: Unité d'Habitation
items.description: The flagship residential housing complex in Marseille that pioneered Brutalist raw-concrete architecture (béton brut). Conceived as a self-contained 'vertical city,' it integrated shops, sports facilities, and a rooftop running track into a single structure.

items.title: Seagram Building
items.artist: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe with Philip Johnson; Kahn & Jacobs (associate architects)
items.description: The Seagram Building places an office tower beside a granite and marble plaza on Park Avenue. Its bronze and tinted-glass curtain wall balances articulated structural members with transparent surfaces. Mies van der Rohe designed the building with Philip Johnson and associate architects Kahn & Jacobs; the official designation report dates its construction to 1956–1958.
items.dateMeaning: Completion endpoint of the official designation report’s “Built 1956–58” construction span; preserve existing 1958 anchor.

items.title: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
items.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's cylindrical, organic architectural monument on Fifth Avenue. Its continuous interior spiral ramp reinvented museum design, allowing visitors to take an elevator to the top and view art along a gentle downward slope.

items.title: TWA Flight Center
items.description: An expressionist landmark at JFK Airport designed to capture the excitement and optimism of Jet Age flight. Its thin-shell concrete roof forms dramatic swooping wings over a fluid, seamless interior.

items.title: Habitat 67
items.attribution: Parcours riverain - Ville de Montréal from Canada
items.description: Habitat 67 is a pioneering urban housing complex designed by architect Moshe Safdie, evolving from his McGill University thesis project. Commissioned for the 1967 World’s Exposition, it presented a humanistic approach to dense urban housing and became an enduring Expo 67 landmark. The realized complex is one manifestation of Safdie’s broader Habitat project; proposals for other locations remained unbuilt iterations.
items.dateMeaning: First opened for Expo 67 in 1967; not a construction-start date. Construction dates and completion date are not established by the retrieved source.

items.title: Nakagin Capsule Tower
items.description: The definitive masterpiece of Japanese Metabolism, featuring 140 prefabricated living modules with circular porthole windows bolted to central concrete cores as adaptable, plug-in urban architecture.

items.title: Sydney Opera House
items.description: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973, the Sydney Opera House brings sculptural form and structural innovation together on Sydney Harbour. Its interlocking vaulted shell groups rise from a platform, housing two principal performance halls and a restaurant. The design emerged from an international competition and responds to its harbour setting.
items.dateMeaning: Official opening/inauguration year, not design date or construction start; construction began in 1959.

items.title: Centre Pompidou
items.description: A High-Tech inside-out building exposing its structural frame, escalators, and color-coded mechanical infrastructure on the exterior facade to maximize uninterrupted interior exhibition space.

items.title: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
items.description: Designed by Frank Gehry, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao occupies a former industrial wharf beside a bend in the Nervión River. Its complex geometry was translated into structure with CATIA software; the exterior combines titanium, limestone, and glass. Construction ran from October 1993 to October 1997, and the museum opened that October.
items.dateMeaning: Opening year; the museum was built October 1993–October 1997, and its grand opening was in October 1997.

items.title: Heydar Aliyev Center
items.artist: Zaha Hadid Architects (design architects; Zaha Hadid credited as architect)
items.description: Designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku sets a continuous, fluid relationship between its public plaza and interior, blurring building envelope and urban landscape. Its cultural program and flowing surface were intended as a contemporary interpretation of Azerbaijani architectural traditions; the complex skin integrates structural and cladding systems.
items.dateMeaning: Official opening ceremony on 10 May 2012, supported by the official event record. ZHA lists a 2007–2012 project span; construction began in 2007.

items.title: Wassily Chair (Model B3)
items.description: Designed while Marcel Breuer was leading the Bauhaus woodwork shop, this landmark piece was inspired by the bent tubular steel of bicycle handlebars. By replacing traditional bulky upholstery with taut leather straps, Breuer stripped the armchair down to its essential geometric form.

items.title: Fauteuil Grand Confort, small model (LC2)
items.artist: Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret, Charlotte Perriand
items.description: Developed by Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret and Charlotte Perriand, the Grand Confort places cushions forming the seat and backrest within an enveloping tubular-metal frame—a construction Charlotte Perriand described as a “cushion basket.” The design came in large and small models and in leather or fabric finishes. The specific small-model Cassina edition shown in the Fondation’s page is a later edition, not necessarily the prototype.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; the museum record labels 1928 as the creation date and classifies its object as a prototype.

items.title: Barcelona Chair
items.artist: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich
items.description: Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed the Barcelona Chair especially for the Barcelona Pavilion. A leather-upholstered metallic profile defines the chair, which remains manufactured and marketed. Its 1929 design date must be distinguished from the manufacturing dates of later surviving examples.
items.dateMeaning: Design date, explicitly “1929 (designed)” in the successfully fetched V&A object record; its probable 1968 manufacture date belongs only to that specimen.

items.title: Diamond Chair
items.description: Harry Bertoia’s Diamond Chair turns welded steel rods into an airy, concave seat-and-back form. Its open wire grid gives the chair a visually light, sculptural character while serving as furniture. Knoll continues the design in varied finishes and optional upholstery; those contemporary configurations should not be mistaken for a single original specification.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; V&A identifies 1952 as designed and 1953 as manufactured, while Knoll labels the chair 1952.

items.title: Braun SK 4 radio-phonograph
items.description: The Braun SK 4 brings a radio and phonograph together in one domestic unit. Dieter Rams and Hans Gugelot are credited as its designers, with Braun as manufacturer. Institutional collections date the model to 1956 and document wood, metal and plastic among its materials. Later related Phonosuper models should not be substituted for this specific design.
items.dateMeaning: Design and manufacture date; institutional records date the SK 4 to 1956. No distinct first launch or exhibition date is established by the retrieved evidence.

items.title: Eames Lounge Chair & Ottoman
items.description: Designed for the Herman Miller furniture company, this piece elevated molded plywood and soft leather into a mid-century luxury staple designed to mimic the feel of a well-worn baseball glove.

items.title: Braun T3 Pocket Radio
items.artist: Dieter Rams and Ulm School of Design (Hochschule für Gestaltung)
items.description: The Braun T3 is a pocket transistor radio designed by Dieter Rams with the Ulm School of Design and made by Braun. Its white plastic casing places the tuning dial below a perforated speaker section. Institutional records date the T3 design to 1958; related T3/4/41 models are grouped together in the Design Museum’s launch chronology.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; institutional sources also place launch of the T3/4/41 pocket-sized transistor radios in 1958.

items.title: Arco Floor Lamp
items.artist: Achille Castiglioni and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni
items.description: Arco emits direct light through a perforated aluminium diffuser mounted on a telescopic stainless-steel stem. Its swivelling reflector is height-adjustable, while a white Carrara-marble base provides the counterbalance and includes a hole for moving it with a wooden pole. Achille and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni adapted street lighting for a domestic setting.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; not a verified first launch or exhibition date.

items.title: Ball Chair
items.description: Eero Aarnio’s Ball Chair (also called the Globe Chair) turns a sphere into an enveloping seat: a sectioned fiberglass shell sits on a revolving pedestal, creating a small, cocoon-like space around the sitter. The design dates to 1963; it debuted at the Cologne Furniture Fair in 1966. Materials and upholstery vary among versions.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; not first launch or manufacture date.

items.title: Panton Chair
items.description: Panton’s chair design was developed over a decade before its 1967 serial-production launch. It is a cantilever chair formed from one piece of synthetic material and has no back legs. The long development involved adapting the concept to the demands of serial production.
items.dateMeaning: First public presentation (August 1967) and start of serial production. Official designer archive gives the broader design development as 1957–1967; preserve the catalog’s 1967 event anchor.

items.title: Valentine Typewriter
items.description: Created for Olivetti, this bright red portable typewriter turned a drab office machine into an anti-academic pop culture fashion statement precursor to modern industrial consumer design.

items.title: Boby Trolley
items.description: Joe Colombo’s Boby is a wheeled, modular storage trolley, originally intended for drawing offices. Its layered construction combines shelves, bins and trays to make flexible storage that can also serve domestic spaces. The V&A identifies its example as injection-moulded ABS plastic; materials and configurations may vary among versions.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; the V&A separately records it as made in 1970.

items.title: Pratone
items.artist: Giorgio Ceretti, Pietro Derossi, and Riccardo Rosso
items.description: Pratone is a seat that replaces conventional upholstery with a cluster of oversized, grass-like blades, turning furniture into a playful landscape. Gufram identifies the designers as Giorgio Ceretti, Pietro Derossi, and Riccardo Rosso, and describes the material as soft polyurethane. The 1971 date is the design/conception date, not a verified date for every production variant.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; Gufram describes it as conceived in 1971. Specific production date not established here.

items.title: Juicy Salif
items.description: Juicy Salif is Philippe Starck’s citrus squeezer for Alessi, formed as a cast-aluminium utensil with a polished finish. Its elongated, splayed legs leave space beneath the reamer for a glass. Alessi dates the design’s production start to 1990; Nationalmuseum distinguishes that design date from its 1999-made collection example.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; Alessi lists production start separately as 1990. Nationalmuseum's example is recorded as made 1999.

items.title: iPhone
items.description: Apple’s first iPhone combined a mobile phone, widescreen iPod, and internet communications device in one handheld product. Its large multi-touch display and finger-operated interface shaped interaction around direct touch rather than a physical keyboard or stylus. This record concerns the first-generation product announced in 2007, not subsequent iPhone models.
items.dateMeaning: Announced/introduced on 9 January 2007, supported by Apple’s press release. U.S. availability planned for June 2007; exact 29 June retail date is not verified in this fetched packet.

items.title: Britons. Join Your Country's Army!
items.description: Alfred Leete’s recruitment poster presents Field Marshal Lord Kitchener facing the viewer, with his right hand pointing outward. Red and black lettering on a white background carries the appeal to join the army. Imperial War Museums dates this printed lithograph and letterpress object to 1914.
items.dateMeaning: First produced in 1914 (not a construction/completion date); catalogued object production date 1914.

items.title: Metropolis Film Poster
items.description: An iconic Art Deco graphic design masterpiece featuring towering geometric skyscrapers and a streamlined metallic robot. It defined sci-fi visual language for a century.

items.title: Futura Typeface
items.description: Futura is a geometric sans-serif typeface designed by Paul Renner for the Bauersche Giesserei. Renner combined classical Roman-capital proportions with elementary geometric construction, while optical adjustments helped balance the letterforms. Developed from 1924, it was launched in 1927. The typeface’s original family and later additions should not be conflated; Futura Inline, Display and Black are distinct later display variants.
items.dateMeaning: First launch/publication (1927); design development began in 1924 and continued through the launch.

items.title: London Underground Map
items.attribution: HI TRICIA! 王 圣 捷

items.title: Normandie
items.description: Cassandre’s colour lithograph advertises the ocean liner Normandie for the Compagnie Générale Transatlantique. A frontal view of the ship’s prow, set against blue sky and green sea, emphasizes its scale and streamlined form; route and class information appears below. Printed in Paris by Alliance Graphique L. Danel.
items.dateMeaning: Printed in 1935; not a design date separately established by the source.

items.title: Keep Calm and Carry On
items.description: The poster places a stylised crown above the separate white title “KEEP CALM AND CARRY ON,” on a red background. IWM records the Ministry of Information as publisher/sponsor but lists the creator as unknown. Its catalogued production date is 1939; the object record does not identify an individual designer.
items.dateMeaning: Production date, not a documented first display. The date of design is not specified more exactly; the poster was not officially sanctioned for display.

items.title: Helvetica (originally Neue Haas Grotesk)
items.artist: Max Miedinger, commissioned and directed by Eduard Hoffmann
items.description: The sans-serif began as Neue Haas Grotesk, developed by Max Miedinger in collaboration with Haas foundry director Eduard Hoffmann. It debuted at Graphic 57 in June 1957. Horizontal stroke terminals, a large x-height and tight spacing created a dense texture. Helvetica became the name for a Linotype adaptation that altered aspects of the original design.
items.dateMeaning: 1957 is the debut of the original Neue Haas Grotesk at Graphic 57, not the later Helvetica naming/rebranding (1960). Work began in autumn 1956; the design was still being revised after its public debut. No construction dates apply.

items.title: Vertigo Poster and Title Sequence
items.artist: Saul Bass (poster/title design); Art Goodman (poster illustration); John H. Whitney (title drawings/animation credit)
items.description: The poster and opening title sequence for Vertigo are related but distinct designs. LACMA identifies Saul Bass as designer and Art Goodman as illustrator of its poster. The opening titles move from a woman’s face toward her eye and then show colored spirals; AFI credits the title drawings to John H. Whitney.
items.dateMeaning: 1958 is the documented poster date and the film's premiere year; exact design completion and title-sequence launch dates are not established.

items.title: Grid Systems in Graphic Design
items.description: Josef Müller-Brockmann’s handbook explains the function and use of grids in two- and three-dimensional graphic design. It provides step-by-step instructions for systems ranging from eight to thirty-two fields, with application examples from business cards to exhibition stands. The grids serve as working tools for organizing and developing visual solutions.
items.dateMeaning: Publication date 1981, explicitly given by Niggli for Grid systems in graphic design. Not the different 1961 book.

items.title: “I Am a Man” Sanitation Strike Poster
items.artist: Memphis sanitation workers and supporters; printed by Allied Printing
items.description: This Memphis sanitation-strike broadside carried the workers’ rallying phrase “I am a man.” The documented example is described as large black lettering on white posterboard and was printed by Allied Printing. Workers and supporters used the phrase during the 1968 strike, demanding suitable compensation and union recognition. Individual signs and reproductions may differ in format and lettering.
items.dateMeaning: 1968; poster date, exact production date not specified by source

items.title: The “Bar” Suit
items.description: Designed for Christian Dior’s first collection, “Bar” paired a fitted, padded-hip jacket with a spreading, pleated skirt. Its silhouette helped define the collection later called the New Look. Museum examples and remakes vary: the V&A’s suit is described as designed in 1947 and possibly remade around 1955.
items.dateMeaning: Design date; the V&A records its example as designed 1947 and possibly made circa 1955.

items.title: Sack Dress / Barrel Line
items.attribution: Staff photographer, Rhode Island School of Design Museum of Art

items.title: Mondrian dress
items.description: Saint Laurent’s Autumn–Winter 1965 collection included cocktail dresses paying homage to Piet Mondrian’s abstract canvases. In a notably restrained, sleeveless silhouette, colored wool-jersey panels and black geometric bands were inlaid to create the graphic effect, with seams concealed from view. The “Mondrian dress” denotes a family of related designs, not one uniform specimen; examples varied in cut and color.
items.dateMeaning: Autumn–Winter 1965 collection, presented 6 August 1965. One museum specimen is seasonally catalogued autumn–winter 1965–1966; this is not a two-year construction/design duration.

items.title: The Miniskirt
items.artist: Mary Quant (central role in popularisation; not established sole inventor)
items.description: Quant helped bring short hemlines from London street style into popular fashion, but the miniskirt was not a single invention: above-the-knee skirts developed gradually, and other designers also showed short styles. The V&A places the miniskirt proper in 1966, when Quant's bright, sporty wool-jersey designs helped popularise the look.
items.dateMeaning: Approximate arrival of the miniskirt proper as a fashion; not a single garment's design, manufacture, launch, or exhibition date.

items.title: Mini-Crini Collection
items.description: Westwood’s Mini-Crini reworked the Victorian crinoline through the proportions of the modern mini-skirt. Its bell-like silhouette fused historic structure with a short skirt length, turning an archival form into a playful contemporary look. The V&A identifies the Mini-Crini collection with 1985; individual ensembles and seasonal labels vary, so this describes the collection rather than one fixed garment.
items.dateMeaning: Collection date (not a documented runway launch date); V&A describes the Mini-Crini as designed for a collection of the same name in 1985.

items.title: Tabi Boots
items.description: Martin Margiela’s Tabi is the house’s first shoe design, presented in its first collection in 1988. Inspired by a fifteenth-century Japanese sock, its split toe was translated into a heeled boot; the red-painted soles left split-toed footprints on the runway. The enduring design has since been reinterpreted in multiple forms and materials.
items.dateMeaning: First presented in Maison Margiela's first collection (1988); design creation date not separately established by retrieved evidence.

items.title: PLEATS PLEASE ISSEY MIYAKE
items.description: PLEATS PLEASE ISSEY MIYAKE developed around Miyake’s garment-pleating process. Garments were cut and sewn oversized, sandwiched between paper and heat-pressed so shaping and pleating occurred together. The official history dates the line’s launch to 1993 and describes clothing intended to be easy to wear, care for and travel with in everyday life.
items.dateMeaning: Line launch in 1993, explicitly stated by the official Miyake English history. Separate standalone-brand/season claim is not part of the approved date anchor.

items.title: Armadillo boot
items.description: Created for Plato’s Atlantis, Alexander McQueen’s sculptural ‘Armadillo’ boot extends and elongates the wearer’s leg with a claw-like profile. The design combines leather and iridescent paillettes; the V&A notes that each boot was hand-carved from wood. Most were show-only pieces rather than intended for commercial production; individual examples and materials vary.
items.dateMeaning: Collection season (Spring/Summer 2010); runway presentation date is not asserted.

contexts.title: First World War
contexts.description: The First World War was a global conflict fought across several continents, at sea and in the air. From 1914 to 1918, it mobilized societies and industry on an unprecedented scale. Its outcome included the disintegration of the Austro-Hungarian, German, Ottoman and Russian empires, reshaping the international order.
contexts.dateMeaning: Approximate conflict span; the war is conventionally dated 1914–1918. The 11 November 1918 armistice ended fighting on the Western Front, not all hostilities or the formal state of war.

contexts.title: World War II
contexts.description: World War II was a global conflict involving more than fifty nations, conventionally dated 1939–1945. The National WWII Museum describes more than one hundred million soldiers deployed. Germany and Japan were among the Axis powers; Britain and the United States were among the Allies. These year boundaries are a broad periodization rather than a universal start event.
contexts.dateMeaning: Conventional 1939–1945 conflict period, supported by the National WWII Museum. Exact geographical start events and precise surrender dates were not verified in this packet.

contexts.title: Moon Landing
contexts.description: Apollo 11’s lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin made the landing, while command module pilot Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit. Armstrong and Aldrin later walked on the Moon and conducted surface exploration.
contexts.dateMeaning: Apollo 11 lunar landing date, 20 July 1969; distinct from launch on July 16 and mission return on July 24.

contexts.title: Bauhaus
contexts.description: The Bauhaus was a school of architecture, design and art founded in Weimar under Walter Gropius. Its teaching joined art and craft through workshops; from 1923, design increasingly engaged with industry and serial production. After moving to Dessau in 1925, its programme continued to evolve under Gropius, Hannes Meyer and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe before closure in 1933.
contexts.artist: Walter Gropius (founding director); institution shaped by Walter Gropius, Hannes Meyer, and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
contexts.dateMeaning: Approximate institutional lifespan: opened/founded in Weimar in April 1919; the school closed in 1933. Not a single work's design or construction date.

contexts.title: Arts & Crafts Movement
contexts.description: An international movement that championed traditional craftsmanship against mass industrialization, favoring natural motifs and decorative honesty.

contexts.title: Mid-Century Modernism
contexts.description: Characterized by clean lines, organic shapes, and democratic mass-production materials like molded plywood, plastic, and fiberglass.
